sentences.text: Tylocephale is a genus of dinosaur belonging to the group Pachycephalosauria, which is part of the larger clade Marginocephalia.
The only known species, T. gilmorei, was named by Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska in 1974 to honor Charles Gilmore, who first described a pachycephalosaur in detail.
This animal was average-sized for its group, reaching about 2 meters in length and weighing roughly 40 kilograms.
Fossils are known only from a skull and parts of the lower jaw, and this specimen possesses the tallest dome recorded among all pachycephalosaurids.
Unlike most dinosaurs that have three skull openings, Tylocephale has only two, and its dome surface had a rough texture rather than a smooth one.
Behind the rounded cranial crest, the neck region featured a cluster of bony projections, while the cheekbones bore large, uneven lumps.
Tylocephale holds the distinction of having the highest dome of any known member of the pachycephalosaur family.
Its teeth possessed high crowns with arched cutting edges, suggesting a diet that might have included nuts, seeds, and insects alongside plants.
Remains were uncovered between 1965 and 1971 by a Polish-Mongolian Expedition working in the Barun Goyot Formation of the Gobi Desert.
Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska formally described the type species in 1974 based on these partial remains.
Serrations on the dentition suggest a potentially heterogeneous diet including leaves, nuts, seeds, and insects.
It has been suggested that Tylocephale utilized a back-and-forth jaw motion, which differs from the up-and-down movement seen in Stegoceras.
The skull dome shows similarities to Pachycephalosaurus, featuring fused sutures, tubercles on the lower jaw and nose, and expanded shelves on the squamosal bone.

Researchers debate whether older individuals of pachycephalosaurs like Tylocephale could engage in head-butting, given that their domes were less vascularized and might have suffered healing complications.
Recent phylogenetic analyses indicate Tylocephale is most closely related to Foraminacephale and Homalocephale, though some researchers have proposed it is a synonym of Prenocephale prenes.
A 2020 cladistic analysis suggested that the lineage of pachycephalosaurs may extend back to the Early Jurassic period.
Tylocephale lived during the Early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 71 million years ago.
The estimated time range for this animal spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago, and it is endemic to the Barun Goyot Formation.
The Barun Goyot Formation was deposited in alluvial plain, lacustrine, and aeolian environments under arid to semiarid climates.
It is debated whether Tylocephale's serrated dentition implies a heterogeneous diet including insects, nuts, and seeds in addition to plants.
